title: Nitzavim: you can return (Deuteronomy 30:1–3)
hook: however far scattered, a person and a people can return

segments.voice: Yesterday, a covenant with those not here this day. Your line was those not yet here. What did you do for someone in the future? Today, a promise for people who drift far. Day five hundred nineteen.

After you've drifted from something, there comes a moment when the distance itself starts to feel like the reason you can't go back. You haven't called a friend in two years, so now it's too awkward to call. You stopped a practice, and starting again feels like admitting you ever stopped. The gap becomes the wall. Deuteronomy thirty is written for people standing on the far side of that gap. And it says, again and again, that the gap is not a wall.
screen: `TWO YEARS WITHOUT A CALL.` → `THE GAP BECOMES THE WALL.` → `THE GAP IS NOT A WALL.`

segments.voice: The chapter imagines the worst. The blessings and the curses have all come true, and the people are scattered among the nations. Then, it says, when you take it to heart there, wherever there is, and return to God and listen with all your heart and all your soul, God will return to you and gather you in. Even, verse four adds, if you've been driven to the far edge of the heavens. The Hebrew root running through these verses is shuv: turn, turn back, return. It comes again and again in a few lines. People return, God returns, the scattered are brought back. From the same root comes teshuvah, usually translated repentance, but closer to returning. It fits that this portion is read in the season just before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, the days most focused on teshuvah. Notice what the text doesn't say. It doesn't say: if you never wander. It assumes the wandering. It sets no distance beyond which return stops working. And notice the order. The people turn first, and then God turns too. A step from one side is met by a step from the other. The medieval teacher Nachmanides reads the verses right after this, about a commandment that isn't too hard or too far away, as being about teshuvah itself. Return, he says, is within reach.
screen: `SCATTERED AMONG THE NATIONS.` · `SHUV: TURN, TURN BACK, RETURN.` · `NO DISTANCE TOO FAR.` · `ONE STEP MET BY ANOTHER.` · then, large: `YOU CAN RETURN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one step back toward something good. Settle, and breathe. Think of something good you've drifted from. A person, a habit, a place, a practice, a part of yourself. Notice the gap, and notice any voice saying it's been too long. Now don't plan the whole road back. Just pick the first step. One message. One page. One walk. One short visit. Picture yourself taking it, and picture it being met. The bell holds the time.
Nitzavim. Standing. And in it, shuv: the turning back that the chapter says is always possible.
Your line: you can return. Today, take the first small step back toward one good thing you've drifted from. Day five hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Teshuvah, returning, is the central theme of the Hebrew month of Elul and the High Holy Days; Deuteronomy 30 is read in synagogue in the weeks just before Rosh Hashanah.

fork.setup: you've been away from something good for years, and it feels far too late. what does Deuteronomy 30 say?
options: past a certain distance, there's no way back.
return, even from the edge of the heavens, and be met.
wait until someone comes to find you.
fork.reveal: the chapter assumes the wandering, sets no limit, and promises the step back will be met.

original.note: Hebrew: return, repentance. from the root shuv, which runs through Deuteronomy 30:1–10.

trapdoor: what you thought: repentance means feeling guilty.
what it means: teshuvah is turning back, and the text says no distance is too far.
what a scholar hears: the root shuv repeats through Deuteronomy 30:1–10, and Nachmanides reads 30:11 as the commandment of teshuvah itself.

notes: Ramban on 30:11 identifies 'this commandment' as teshuvah; paraphrased.
The script avoids giving an exact count of shuv-root words in 30:1–10 (often given as seven); Keeper may add it if desired.
